lessons.title: Measuring turns

steps.headline: An angle measures a turn, and a full turn is 360°.

lead.text: Turn on the spot until you face the way you started. That is a full turn. We cut it into 360 tiny equal turns called degrees (°).
Half a turn is a straight line. A quarter-turn is the corner of a page, called a right angle.
A full turn is 360° and a half-turn is 180°.
A ray splits the corner of a page into two angles. Between them the two angles fill the whole right angle.

reveal.text: You took the part you knew from the whole corner. Angles that fill a corner always add to 90°.

steps.headline: A straight line is split into two angles. One is 41°. Find the other.

workedSteps.text: A straight line is a half-turn, 180°. The two angles fill it.

steps.headline: Two angles on a straight line. One is 68°. Find the other.

lead.text: A full turn takes you all the way round. A pointer that stops part of the way still has some turn left.

reveal.text: A full turn is 360°. You took the 140° already made from it, as you took a part from 90° and from 180°.

lead.text: Picture a door swinging open from closed. Is how far it has swung decided by how wide the door is?

lessons.orientation: Use quarter, half and full turns to find an unknown angle.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A skater spins half a turn, then another quarter-turn. She wants to finish facing the way she started.

intro.promise: By the end you'll measure turns in degrees and find an unknown angle in a corner, on a line and round a point.

recap.keyIdea: An angle measures a turn. Parts of a right angle add to 90°, on a straight line to 180°, round a point to 360°.

blocks.text: You worked out that a skater who has made half a turn and a quarter-turn needs 1 more quarter-turn.
You found 112° beside 68° on a line, and 220° left of a full turn after 140°.

recap.nextHook: Three angles fill a straight line in a triangle too. Find out how they add up inside one.

lessons.title: Angles in triangles

steps.headline: The three angles of a triangle always add to 180°.

lead.text: Tear off the three corners of a paper triangle and put them side by side. They fill a straight line, so they make 180°.
This works for every triangle. A triangle with one right angle is called a right triangle.
Three angles, one total: 180°.
Two angles of this triangle are marked. The third corner fills what is left of the 180°.

reveal.text: You took the two angles you knew from 180°. Any triangle's missing angle works this way.

steps.headline: A right triangle has another angle of 20°. Find the third angle.

workedSteps.text: The right angle takes 90° of the 180°.

steps.headline: A right triangle has another angle of 32°. Find the third angle.

lead.text: Some triangles have two angles the same size. Take the third angle from 180°, then share what is left between the two equal angles.

reveal.text: You split the leftover 180° between two equal angles. Subtract first, then share.

lead.text: A student wants to draw a triangle with two right angles. Test the angles against the total before drawing.

lessons.orientation: Find a missing triangle angle and test whether angle measures are possible.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You tear the three corners off a paper triangle and set them side by side, points touching. They fit exactly along a straight edge. Two corners measure 70° and 50°.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a missing angle in any triangle and tell whether three angles could make one.

recap.keyIdea: The three angles of a triangle add to 180°, so any missing angle is 180° minus the others.

blocks.text: You found that corners of 70° and 50° leave 60° of the straight edge.
You also found 58° in a right triangle with a 32° angle, and 68° for each equal angle beside 44°.

recap.nextHook: Triangles are one kind of shape. Next, measure how much flat space any shape covers.

lessons.title: Boundary and area

steps.headline: Perimeter is the way round. Area is the space inside.

lead.text: Walk round the edge of a shape and the length you walk is its perimeter.
Cover the inside with unit squares and the number of squares is its area, in square units such as square metres (m²).
Perimeter is a length. Area counts squares.
Look at both rectangles. Add the sides round each one, and turn on the unit squares to count what is inside.

reveal.text: You compared the boundaries and the squares. Equal perimeters do not mean equal areas.

steps.headline: A rectangle is 7 m by 2 m. Find its perimeter and its area.

workedSteps.text: Add all four sides: two of each length.

steps.headline: A rectangle is 6 m by 4 m. Find its perimeter and its area.

lead.text: Imagine the squares in rows, then count.

reveal.text: Rows times squares in each row. It works for any rectangle.

lead.text: Two lengths and two widths make 20 m of fence, so one length and one width add to 10 m. The sides must be whole numbers.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish distance around a shape from the surface it covers.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A floor is covered in square tiles: 3 rows, with 5 tiles in each row.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell the distance round a rectangle from the space inside it, and find both.

recap.keyIdea: Perimeter is the distance round a shape and area counts the squares inside. For a rectangle: add the sides, and multiply them.

blocks.text: You counted 15 tiles in 3 rows of 5.
You found that 6 by 4 and 8 by 2 rectangles share a perimeter but not an area, and that 20 m of fence can enclose up to 25 m².

recap.nextHook: Rectangles are easy to count in rows. A slanted triangle is harder: which length do you use?

lessons.title: Base and height

steps.headline: The height of a triangle is measured at a right angle to its base.

lead.text: Pick any side of the triangle as its base. The height is the straight distance from the opposite corner to the line of the base, meeting it at a right angle.
The height is not a sloping side. It is the shortest way across.
This triangle has base 8 cm and height 5 cm. Picture the rectangle with the same base and height. The triangle covers half of it.

reveal.text: You halved base × height. That is the rule for every triangle.

lead.text: Slide the top corner along a line parallel to the base. The sloping sides change length.

reveal.text: Only the base and the height matter to the area. Neither changed.

steps.headline: A triangle has base 9 cm and perpendicular height 4 cm. Find its area.

workedSteps.text: Use the base and the perpendicular height, not a sloping side.
Halve it: a triangle is half the rectangle.

steps.headline: A parallelogram has base 8 cm and height 5 cm. Find its area.

workedSteps.text: A diagonal cuts it into two equal triangles.
Two triangles together make the parallelogram.

lead.text: Choose the base and the height. Check the height meets the base at a right angle.

reveal.text: Base × height, halved. The same steps as the 9 by 4 triangle.

lead.text: You know the area and the base this time, not the height. Base × height ÷ 2 gives the area.

lessons.orientation: Measure perpendicular height and connect triangle area to a parallelogram.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A rectangular card is 6 cm by 4 cm. It is cut along a diagonal into two identical triangles.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a triangle's area from its base and perpendicular height, and use the same idea for a parallelogram.

recap.keyIdea: A triangle's area is half of base × perpendicular height, and a parallelogram's is base × perpendicular height.

blocks.text: You found that half of a 6 by 4 card is 12 cm².
You showed that sliding a triangle's top corner leaves its area alone, and that a 30 m² flag with a 10 m base stands 6 m tall.

recap.nextHook: Some shapes are built from several parts. Next, split a shape into pieces you can measure.

lessons.title: Pieces and cutouts

steps.headline: Split a shape into pieces, or take a cutout from a bigger rectangle.

lead.text: Many shapes are rectangles joined together, or a rectangle with a corner missing. There are two ways in.
Add the areas of pieces that fit together without overlapping. Or work out the whole rectangle and subtract the missing part.
Either way, every part of the shape is counted exactly once.
This L-shaped floor fits inside a 9 m by 7 m rectangle. The missing corner is 3 m by 2 m.

reveal.text: You took the missing corner from the whole rectangle. What remains is the floor.

steps.headline: A floor is a 5 m by 4 m rectangle with a 3 m by 2 m rectangle joined to it. Find its area.

workedSteps.text: Add them. The pieces do not overlap.

steps.headline: A 12 cm by 8 cm rectangle has a 5 cm by 3 cm corner removed. Find the area left.

workedSteps.text: Find the area of the whole rectangle.
Find the area of the cutout.

lead.text: Two rectangles are joined, edge to edge. Find the area of each, then combine them.

reveal.text: Pieces that do not overlap: add. A cutout: subtract. Both count every part once.

steps.headline: Two trapezoids fit together into one parallelogram.

lead.text: A trapezoid has one pair of parallel sides, called its bases.
Flip a copy and join it to the first. The two make one parallelogram, whose base is the two bases added.
The parallelogram has the same height as one trapezoid. Its area is its base times the height. One trapezoid is half of it.

lessons.orientation: Calculate area by combining simple pieces or subtracting a missing corner.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A hall is 10 m long and 6 m wide, but a 4 m by 3 m corner of it is missing, leaving an L shape.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the area of an L shape two ways, and of a trapezoid by building a parallelogram.

recap.keyIdea: Add the areas of pieces that do not overlap, or subtract a cutout from the whole. A trapezoid is half a parallelogram.

blocks.text: You found that a 10 m by 6 m hall with a 4 m by 3 m corner missing covers 48 m².
You also found 22 m² for a patio from two pieces and 32 cm² for a trapezoid with bases 10 and 6.

recap.nextHook: A circle has no straight sides to split into rectangles. Find out what its edge and its inside need.

lessons.title: Around and inside circles

steps.headline: A diameter is two radii laid end to end.

lead.text: The radius runs from the centre of a circle to its edge. The diameter runs from edge to edge through the centre.
Radius and diameter measure different lengths. Check which one you are given.

steps.headline: The distance round a circle is about 3.14 times the distance across.

lead.text: The distance round a circle is its circumference. Divide it by the diameter and you always get the same number, π, about 3.14.
So circumference = π × diameter. In radius terms, that is 2 × π × radius.

steps.headline: A circle has radius 5 cm. Find its circumference. Use π ≈ 3.14.

workedSteps.text: Double the radius to get the diameter.

steps.headline: A circle has radius 3 cm. Find its circumference. Use π ≈ 3.14.
The space inside a circle is π × radius × radius.

lead.text: Area is the space inside, so it has square units. It uses the radius twice: π × r × r.
Square the radius, then multiply by π. Never use the diameter in place of the radius.
The mat's size is given across. Decide whether that is the radius or the diameter before you start.

reveal.text: Halve the diameter, square the radius, multiply by π. Using 8 as the radius would have made the area four times too big.

lead.text: Compare 2 × π × r with π × r × r. Ask how many times the radius appears in each.

lessons.orientation: Use radius and diameter correctly in circumference and circle-area calculations.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A pizza has a 15 cm line from its middle to its edge.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the distance round a circle and the space inside it, from either its radius or its diameter.

recap.keyIdea: The circumference is π × diameter and the area is π × radius × radius. Check which of radius and diameter you are given.

blocks.text: You found that a 15 cm middle-to-edge line makes a pizza 30 cm across.
You found 18.84 cm round a circle of radius 3 cm, and 50.24 m² for a mat 8 m across.

recap.nextHook: A bigger copy of a shape changes lengths and areas differently. Find out how much.

lessons.title: Same shape, new size

steps.headline: A similar shape is an enlargement or reduction: every length is multiplied by the same scale factor.

lead.text: Two shapes are similar when one is a scaled copy of the other. Their angles match, and each length is the matching original length times one number.
That number is the scale factor. Matching lengths, such as height with height, are called corresponding. To find the factor, divide a copy's length by the matching original length.
A designer wants a bigger copy of a rectangle that keeps its shape exactly. She is choosing what to do to the sides.

reveal.text: One factor on every side keeps the shape. You chose multiplying every length, not changing one length or adding the same amount.

steps.headline: A rectangle 2 units wide and 3 units tall is enlarged by scale factor 4. Find the new width and height.

workedSteps.text: Multiply the width by the factor.
Multiply the height by the same factor.

steps.headline: The same rectangle, 2 units wide and 3 units tall, is enlarged by scale factor 3. Find the new width and height.

workedSteps.text: Multiply the width by the factor.
Multiply the height by the same factor.

lead.text: This time the factor isn't given. Match a side of the new triangle with its corresponding side in the old one.

reveal.text: You found the factor from the shortest sides, then used it on the longest. One factor, every side.

lead.text: A photograph is printed small enough for a wallet. Each length shrinks by the same factor.

lessons.orientation: Match corresponding lengths and apply one scale factor to every dimension.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A photo is 4 cm wide and 3 cm tall. It is enlarged so that it is 8 cm wide.

intro.promise: By the end you'll scale a shape up or down with one factor and find the factor from matching sides.

recap.keyIdea: Similar shapes have the same angles, and every length is multiplied by the same scale factor.

blocks.text: You found that a 4 by 3 photo enlarged to 8 wide stands 6 cm tall.
You also found a longest side of 15 cm from a shortest side of 9 cm, and 2.5 for a width of 5 halved.

recap.nextHook: Lengths scale by the factor. Does the area scale the same way?

lessons.title: When area scales

steps.headline: Scale every length by k and the area is scaled by k × k.

lead.text: Area is made from two lengths, a length and a width. A scale factor works on both of them.
So the factor acts twice on the area. We call the result the area factor.
Length factor k gives area factor k × k.
The rectangle starts at 3 cm by 2 cm. Both of its lengths are doubled.

reveal.text: You scaled both lengths, then found the area. The area grew by more than the lengths did.

steps.headline: A shape has area 8 cm². Every length is tripled. Find the new area.

workedSteps.text: The area factor is the length factor squared.
Multiply the area by the area factor.

steps.headline: A shape has area 6 cm². Every length is tripled. Find the new area.

lead.text: You don't need the new lengths. Use the length factor to get the area factor.

reveal.text: The area factor came from the length factor alone. No new side lengths were needed.

lead.text: Squaring multiplies a number by itself. Going back asks which number, times itself, gives the area factor.
A designer stretches a banner in one direction only. Check which lengths actually change.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish a length scale factor from the resulting area factor.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A square tile is 2 cm by 2 cm. A bigger copy is made with every side twice as long.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find how area changes when every length is scaled, and go back from an area factor to a length factor.

recap.keyIdea: If every length is multiplied by k, the area is multiplied by k × k.

blocks.text: You found that a tile with doubled sides holds 4 of the small tiles.
You also found 54 cm² when an area of 6 cm² has its lengths tripled, and 3 as the factor behind 9 times the area.

recap.nextHook: Squared lengths also add up in a right triangle. Find out how.

lessons.title: Right-triangle distances

steps.headline: In a right triangle, the squares of the two legs add to the square of the longest side.

lead.text: The two sides that meet at the right angle are the legs. The longest side, across from the right angle, is the hypotenuse.
Call the legs a and b and the hypotenuse c. Then a² + b² = c². A square root undoes squaring: the square root of 49 is 7, because 7 × 7 = 49.
Use a² + b² = c². Square both legs and add them. That gives c², so a square root gives c.

reveal.text: You squared both legs, added, then took the square root. The straight side is shorter than the two legs added.

steps.headline: The legs are 3 m and 4 m. Find the hypotenuse, the shortcut.
A right triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Find its hypotenuse.

lead.text: Check which sides are the legs before you square.

reveal.text: The same three moves as before: square, add, root.

steps.headline: With the hypotenuse known, subtract to find a missing leg.

lead.text: Sometimes the hypotenuse is given and a leg is missing. Start from a² + b² = c² and move a² to the other side.
The missing leg's square is c² minus the known leg's square. Then take the square root.
This time the hypotenuse is known. Check which side it is before you subtract.

lessons.orientation: Find a missing side using squared lengths and identify when the Pythagorean theorem applies.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You walk 3 m east, then 4 m north. A friend says you could have cut straight across instead.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the longest side of a right triangle from the other two, and a missing leg from the longest.

recap.keyIdea: In a right triangle a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse. Add the squares of the legs, or subtract the known leg's square.

blocks.text: You found that the straight shortcut is shorter than the 7 m bent path, and that it comes to 5 m.
You also found a hypotenuse of 13 m from legs 5 m and 12 m, and a missing leg of 24 cm.

recap.nextHook: Right triangles also measure distances on a grid. Find out how.

lessons.title: Distance on a grid

steps.headline: The gap between two points is the difference of their coordinates.

lead.text: A point (x, y) says how far across and how far up it is. The horizontal gap between two points is the difference of their x coordinates.
The vertical gap is the difference of their y coordinates. If a coordinate is negative, count across zero: from −2 to 3 is 5 units.
Use the y coordinates this time, which tell you how far up each point is.

reveal.text: You subtracted the y coordinates. The same move works across a grid in either direction.

steps.headline: Find the straight-line distance from (1, 1) to (9, 16).

workedSteps.text: They are the legs of a right triangle. Square and add.

steps.headline: Find the straight-line distance from A (1, 2) to B (4, 6).

lead.text: Find how far apart the points are in each direction first.

reveal.text: The same four moves as before: differences, squares, sum, root.

lead.text: Both ends of a segment are moved: 2 units right and 1 unit up. Ask what happens to the gaps between them.

lessons.orientation: Use coordinate differences as right-triangle legs and distinguish direct distance from a grid path.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A drone on a grid flies from A (1, 2) to B (4, 6). It goes east first, then north.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find how far apart two points are in a straight line, from their coordinates.

recap.keyIdea: Subtract coordinates to get the horizontal and vertical gaps, then use them as the legs of a right triangle.

blocks.text: You found that the drone's bent route is 7 units, and the straight line from A to B is 5.
You also found 17 units from (1, 1) to (9, 16), and 25 from (0, 1) to (7, 25).

recap.nextHook: Flat shapes have areas. Next, fill a box and count the space inside it.

lessons.title: Filling space

steps.headline: Volume counts the cubes that fill a space.

lead.text: Fill a box with unit cubes. The number of cubes is its volume, in cubic units such as cubic centimetres (cm³).
A unit cube has a length, a width and a height, so volume needs three directions. Area needs two. A length needs one.
This box is 4 cm long, 3 cm wide and 2 cm high. Picture one layer of unit cubes, then the layers stacked on it.

reveal.text: You counted one layer, then stacked layers. Length × width × height counts every cube once.

steps.headline: A box is 6 cm long, 2 cm wide and 4 cm high. Find its volume.

workedSteps.text: Find the cubes in one layer.

steps.headline: A box is 4 cm long, 3 cm wide and 5 cm high. Find its volume.

workedSteps.text: Find the cubes in one layer.

lead.text: Count one layer, then stack the layers.

reveal.text: One layer, then the layers stacked. Any order of the three lengths gives the same volume.

lead.text: Volume is the base area times the height. When the height is the missing piece, undo the multiplying.
A cube has three equal edges. Use its side in all three places.

lessons.orientation: Count volume in cubic units and predict how it changes when dimensions change.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A box holds sugar cubes in layers. Each layer has 2 rows of 5 cubes, and 3 layers are stacked.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the volume of a box in cubic units, and its height when you know the volume.

recap.keyIdea: Volume is length × width × height, in cubic units. Divide by the base area to find a missing height.

blocks.text: You counted 30 cubes in 3 layers of 10.
You also found 60 cm³ for a 4 by 3 by 5 box and 216 cm³ for a cube of side 6 cm.

recap.nextHook: A box has an outside as well as an inside. Unfold it to find the surface.

lessons.title: Unfolding surface area

steps.headline: Surface area is the total area of every face, and a box has three matching pairs.

lead.text: Cut a box along its edges and flatten it. The flat shape is its net. It shows every face.
The total area of all the faces is the surface area. Top and base match, front and back match, left and right match.

steps.headline: A closed box is 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm. Find its surface area.

workedSteps.text: Add them, then double for the matching faces.

steps.headline: A closed box is 5 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm. Find its surface area.

lead.text: Some boxes have no lid. Find the area of the closed box first.

reveal.text: Closed total, minus the missing face. Only the face that is missing comes off.

lead.text: Count the lengths multiplied together in an area, and in a volume.

lessons.orientation: Unfold a box to calculate covering area, including the effect of a missing lid.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A cube-shaped gift box has sides 3 cm long. She wraps it in paper with no overlaps.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the surface area of a box by unfolding it, with or without a lid.

recap.keyIdea: Surface area is the total area of all faces: twice the sum of three different faces, less any face that is missing.

blocks.text: You found that a cube of side 3 cm needs 54 cm² of paper.
You also found 62 cm² for a 5 by 3 by 2 box, and 47 cm² when its lid is missing.

recap.nextHook: You can now measure lengths, areas, volumes and surfaces. Put them together on a harder shape.

questions.prompt: A 90° corner contains a 35° angle. How many degrees remain?
hints: Identify the total turn of the corner.
Subtract the known part from the total.
Calculate 90 − 35.
questions.onCorrect: The two parts fill the corner, so they add to 90°. Take the part you know from the whole.

misconceptions.feedback: 35° is the part you were given. The question asks for the part that is left.
That adds the 35° to the corner. The two parts together make the corner, not more.

questions.prompt: Two adjacent angles form a straight line. One is 68°. What is the other, in degrees?
hints: A straight line represents a half-turn.
The adjacent angles add to 180°.
Calculate 180 − 68.
questions.onCorrect: The other angle is 180° − 68° = 112°: the two angles fill the half-turn.

misconceptions.feedback: 68° is the angle you were given. Find the part that is left.
That adds 180 to 68. The whole is 180°, so the other part is smaller than that.

questions.prompt: A pointer has turned 140°. How many more degrees complete a full 360° turn in the same direction?
hints: Use a full turn as the total.
Find the turn that has not yet been made.
Calculate 360 − 140.
questions.onCorrect: 220°. The turn so far and the turn left make a full 360°.

misconceptions.feedback: 140° is the turn already made. Find the part still to come.
That is 180 − 140. A full turn is 360°, not 180°.

questions.prompt: The arms of an angle are drawn twice as long, along the same lines. What happens to its size in degrees?
hints: Separate the length of a ray from its direction.

acceptedIdeas: It stays the same
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The degree measure depends on the directions of the rays, so extending them leaves the angle unchanged.

questions.onCorrect: The angle stays the same. It measures how far you turn, not how long the arms are.

misconceptions.feedback: A longer arm covers more paper, not more turn. The directions of the arms haven't changed.
Nothing was cut. The arms point the same way, so the turn is the same.

questions.prompt: A right angle is split into 27° and another angle. Find the other angle in degrees.
hints: A right angle is the whole.
Subtract the part already given.
Calculate 90 − 27.
questions.onCorrect: 63°. The parts of a right angle add to 90°, so subtract the part you know.

misconceptions.feedback: 117° comes from starting at 180°. A right angle is a quarter-turn, so start from 90°.
27° is the part you were given. Find the other part.

questions.prompt: Which pair can form a straight angle?
hints: Add each pair and compare with a half-turn.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 72° + 108° = 180°, the measure of a straight angle.

questions.onCorrect: 72° + 108° = 180°. Two angles on a straight line fill a half-turn.

misconceptions.feedback: Those add to 90°, a right angle. A straight angle is a half-turn.
Those add to more than a half-turn: 190°.

questions.prompt: A triangle has angles 48° and 67°. What is its third angle in degrees?
hints: All three angles of a triangle together make 180°.
Add the two angles you are given.
Subtract 48 + 67 from 180.
questions.onCorrect: 65°. Take the two angles you know from 180°.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the two angles added. The third angle is what is left of 180°.
That leaves out the 67° angle. All three angles share the total.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has another angle of 32°. Find its third angle in degrees.
hints: The right angle uses half of the triangle's total.
The two acute angles add to 90°.
Calculate 90 − 32.
questions.onCorrect: 58°. Take the right angle and the 32° from 180°. The two sharp angles share 90°.

misconceptions.feedback: 90° is the right angle you already have. Find the third angle.
That leaves out the right angle. Take it from 180° as well.
